Solution:

(a) Fix seed s of length k. Build a full binary tree of depth k. Label the root (level 0) with s. Rule: if a vertex is labeled r, its left child is labeled G0(r) and its right child G1(r). Since |G0(r)| = |G1(r)| = |r|, every vertex at every level carries a k-bit label. For x = x1…xk ∈ {0,1}^k define fs(x) as the label of the leaf reached by starting at the root and, for i = 1,…,k, going left if xi = 0 and right if xi = 1. Closed form: fs(x1…xk) = G_{x_k}(⋯G_{x_2}(G_{x_1}(s))⋯), where G_{x_1} is applied first at the root and the composition is read inner-to-outer (G_0/G_1 select left/right halves of the current expansion).

(b) Cost: the walk has exactly k = |x| edges. To take the edge out of a vertex labeled r toward child b ∈ {0,1}, one evaluation of G on input r produces the pair (G0(r), G1(r)); keeping half gives the child's label. Labels along the path have length k throughout, so each call is on a k-bit string. Hence evaluating fs(x) uses exactly d = |x| applications of G — for inputs of length d ≤ k this is d calls; in the theorem's family d = k. This is O(d) calls, and each call runs in poly(k) time (G is a PRG, hence polynomial-time); the path has d+1 labels, so total time is d · poly(k) = poly(k, d). No other tree vertices are ever computed: the other 2^{d+1} − d − 2 vertices are never materialized.

(c) A function {0,1}^k → {0,1}^k assigns a k-bit value to each of the 2^k inputs: its truth table has 2^k entries totaling k·2^k bits — exponential in k. The GGM seed s is a k-bit description of one such function: together with the (fixed, public) evaluation algorithm and the tree rule, s determines fs completely, so an exponential object is represented by a linear-size program. This compression is only useful because $f_s$ is pseudorandom: the family contains only $2^k$ functions (one per seed), whereas the number of all functions $\{0,1\}^k \to \{0,1\}^k$ is $(2^k)^{2^k}$ — astronomically larger — and yet no efficient oracle machine can tell a uniformly chosen member of the family from a truly random function.

Solution:

Reduction. Suppose PPT D distinguishes {G(U_k)} from {U_{kℓ(k)}} with non-negligible gap δ(k). Define an oracle machine M^h: query h at the fixed points a1,…,a_{ℓ(k)} (at most ℓ(k) = poly(k) queries — allowed for a PPT oracle machine), concatenate the answers into z ∈ {0,1}^{kℓ(k)}, and output D(z). If h = f_s for uniform s, then z = fs(a1)⋯fs(a_{ℓ(k)}) = G(s), so Pr[M^{f_{U_k}}(1^k) = 1] = Pr[D(G(U_k)) = 1]. If h = F is a truly random function, then since a1,…,a_{ℓ(k)} are distinct, the values F(a1),…,F(a_{ℓ(k)}) are independent uniform k-bit strings, so z is uniform over {0,1}^{kℓ(k)}: Pr[M^{F_k}(1^k) = 1] = Pr[D(U_{kℓ(k)}) = 1]. The distinguishing gap transfers exactly, contradicting Definition 2.17. Hence G is a PRG.

Why distinctness matters: if a_i = a_j, then under a random F the answers F(a_i), F(a_j) are equal (same value), while under fs they are also equal — but the concatenation would no longer be uniform under the random function, breaking the simulation of U_{kℓ(k)}. Distinct inputs guarantee the random function's answers are independent. (We need ℓ(k) ≤ 2^k distinct strings, which holds for all sufficiently large k; finitely many small k can be ignored.) The argument uses the oracle form of the definition in an essential way: the distinguisher D is turned into an oracle machine that is allowed poly(k) queries — a power the single-sample PRG definition does not grant.

Why PRF is strictly stronger. Combined with Theorem 2.18 (PRG ⇒ PRF), the trivial direction shows pseudorandom functions exist iff pseudorandom generators exist — the two existence notions coincide (both are equivalent to the existence of one-way functions, Theorem 2.14). But the object is strictly more powerful: a PRF gives polynomial-time random access to exponentially many pseudorandom values (2^k values, any of them computable on demand), whereas a PRG gives one pseudorandom string that must be generated in full — producing 2^k pseudorandom values by scanning a generator output would take exponential time. That a mere generator can be 'upgraded' to such an object is precisely the nontrivial content of GGM, and it is what makes PRFs the workhorse of symmetric cryptography (shared seed ⇒ shared random-looking function) and of complexity-theoretic barriers such as Natural Proofs.

Solution:

(a) An oracle machine M is adaptive if the points it queries may be chosen as a function of the answers it has already received (its full query history); non-adaptive machines fix all queries in advance. Definition 2.17 places no restriction on M beyond being probabilistic polynomial-time, so adaptive strategies are included — and since every non-adaptive machine is a special case of an adaptive one, allowing adaptivity can only make the indistinguishability requirement harder to satisfy, hence the definition is as strong (pessimistic) as possible. This is not mere paranoia: in cryptography the distinguisher models an attacker, and real attacks are adaptive. For example, in a chosen-message attack on a message-authentication code built from a PRF, the forger requests tags of messages it selects after seeing earlier tags (forging fs(m) for a fresh m requires queries whose choice depends on previous answers); an encryption adversary may likewise choose plaintexts depending on previously observed ciphertexts. A notion that only excluded or limited adaptivity would fail to capture such attacks. (One can even show settings — e.g., testing structured function families — where adaptive tests are strictly more powerful than non-adaptive ones with the same query budget.)

(b) The single output bit is the canonical form of a hypothesis test: M is asked to decide between two possible worlds — oracle = fs for uniform s, or oracle = a truly random function — and |Pr[M^{f_{U_k}} = 1] − Pr[M^{F_k} = 1]| measures exactly how well M can tell them apart. A strategy that outputs several bits, or a real-valued score, is converted as follows: fix the acceptance rule of your experiment (e.g., 'succeed iff the output equals the right answer', or 'accept iff the score exceeds a threshold') and let M output 1 exactly when the rule accepts; the success/advantage of the original strategy is, by definition, the difference in probability of this binary event between the two worlds, so nothing is lost — thresholding a real-valued test at its optimum point preserves the advantage up to the standard gap, and any comparison between the two worlds is a comparison of two probabilities of a binary predicate. In short: the power of the distinguisher lives entirely in its queries (adaptivity, number of queries, computation between queries); the final answer is just a vote, and one bit suffices to vote. (This is why the definition quantifies over machines outputting one bit, yet GGM's hybrids and reductions — e.g., Exercise m5ggm-ex-2 — may freely use poly(k) queries: queries are where the work happens.)
